# Snapshots are assembled shard by shard, not frozen

Go cannot fork, so there is no cheap copy-on-write image of the store, and taking the global write lock long enough to serialise a large store would stall every caller for hundreds of milliseconds. Instead each shard is serialised under its own read lock, and the snapshot header records the log sequence number reached by each shard.

## Consequences

- The snapshot is not a single point in time; shards in it are internally consistent but mutually skewed.
- Recovery corrects for this by replaying the log from the **lowest** sequence in the header, but it does not blindly re-apply what it reads. Each record is routed to the shard its key hashes to and suppressed if that shard's header sequence already covers it. Re-application is not harmless — a record older than the snapshot state for its key would overwrite a newer value — so the per-shard filter is the mechanism, not an optimisation over one.
- A snapshot serialized from memory records the eviction generation before reading shards and revalidates it under the eviction-path interlock before rename; an attempt that a live-entry eviction overtook is discarded rather than installed, and serialization itself still takes only per-shard read locks. A snapshot reconstructed from the log is exempt by construction, because its contents come from the log rather than from live shards and no eviction can invalidate them.
- Once a live entry has been evicted, automatic compaction no longer snapshots the capacity-constrained in-memory view. The writer rolls to a new segment, a background pass reconstructs the durable image through the closed WAL prefix, and only that prefix can be pruned after installation. Writes continue in the new segment while reconstruction runs.
- After eviction, final shutdown reconstruction processes one configured shard at a time. This bounds additional live-entry memory by the largest durable shard rather than a second full store, at the cost of reading the snapshot and retained WAL once per configured shard before writing the final image.
- The successful-snapshot counter marks completed installation and cleanup: rename, directory synchronization, removal of superseded snapshots, and removal of covered segments. Post-rename failures identify the snapshot as installed but do not increment the counter.
- The header carries the shard count as an explicit field alongside the per-shard sequences. A store reopened with a different shard count keeps the snapshot as its base image but cannot map the old per-shard replay positions onto the new shards. It safely skips only through the lowest header sequence, then replays every retained record after that point.
- The install sequence is rename, directory sync, then cleanup — and on Windows the directory sync is a documented no-op, because the standard library exposes no portable flushable directory handle. The file itself is fsynced before rename there, so a Windows store is one link weaker in this chain than a Unix one. Accepted rather than papered over with a dependency; see ADR 0008.
